ov_en: TE-TE smuggling occurs when both front-end and back-end support Transfer-Encoding but handle obfuscated TE variants differently. Attackers craft a TE header with mixed case or special characters so one endpoint recognizes chunked while the other falls back to Content-Length, creating a parsing discrepancy.
vu_en: Servers disagree on handling non-standard TE header formats: one strictly matches the "chunked" keyword (rejecting obfuscation), the other parses it leniently (accepting obfuscated variants).
ex_en: 1. Enumerate TE obfuscation variants 2. Find the variant that causes front-end/back-end parsing to diverge 3. Craft smuggling payload 4. Use smuggling to bypass security controls or hijack requests/poison cache
mi_en: Strictly normalize TE header handling; reject non-standard TE formats; unify HTTP parsing logic across front-end and back-end; use end-to-end HTTP/2 to eliminate smuggling risk; deploy request smuggling detection rules.

ov_en: Developers often restrict redirects via regex or blacklists, which can be bypassed with multiple techniques.
vu_en: Validation logic is too loose and can be bypassed via encoding, special characters, or IP format variants.
ex_en: Use encoding, special characters, or IP format variations to bypass domain-based redirect restrictions.
mi_en: Use strict allowlist validation on the destination domain.

ov_en: Open redirect combined with SSRF is an advanced bypass technique. When SSRF filtering only checks the initial URL domain/IP (allowlist) but the server-side HTTP client follows 302 redirects, attackers can use the target's own open redirect endpoint as a pivot to redirect requests from an allowlisted domain to an internal IP.
vu_en: Prerequisites: 1) Target has an open redirect vulnerability 2) SSRF URL filtering only checks the initial request domain/IP 3) Server-side HTTP client auto-follows 302/301 redirects 4) Redirected requests are not re-filtered.
ex_en: 1. Find an open redirect endpoint 2. Confirm SSRF entry point 3. Craft redirect URL pointing to internal target 4. Use redirect URL as SSRF input 5. Bypass allowlist via redirect to access internal resources
mi_en: 1. Fix all open redirect vulnerabilities 2. Re-filter SSRF on every hop of HTTP request chain 3. Disable auto-redirect following in HTTP client 4. Both allowlist and blacklist filtering 5. Network-level isolation for servers hosting SSRF functionality

ov_en: Clickjacking combined with XSS escalates two client-side vulnerabilities together. A standalone Self-XSS has limited impact (requires victim to paste the payload themselves), but combined with clickjacking it becomes remotely exploitable via multi-step user guidance.
vu_en: 1) Target has a Self-XSS or reflected XSS vulnerability 2) Target has no X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors 3) Each vulnerability has limited standalone impact, but the combination escalates severity significantly.
ex_en: 1. Find Self-XSS entry point (e.g., profile edit page) 2. Confirm target allows iframe embedding 3. Build multi-step clickjacking page 4. Pre-populate XSS payload via clipboard API 5. Guide user through the edit-paste-submit action chain
mi_en: 1. Set X-Frame-Options: DENY 2. Fix all XSS (including Self-XSS) 3. Strictly HTML-encode all input 4. Configure CSP to restrict inline script execution 5. Use CSRF tokens on sensitive operations

ov_en: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object References) is the core vulnerability type for OWASP A01:2021 Broken Access Control. When an application accesses database objects via user-controlled input (e.g., user_id, order_id) without verifying the current user's authorization, attackers can enumerate parameter values to access others' data, modify others' info, or escalate privileges.
vu_en: Root cause: missing fine-grained authorization checks on the backend. Common scenarios: (1) API queries DB using IDs from URL path or query params; (2) Backend only verifies login but not resource ownership; (3) Predictable sequential IDs instead of UUIDs; (4) Frontend hides the entry point but backend has no check.
ex_en: 1. Log in with two test accounts A and B with different permissions 2. Intercept A's API requests and record all endpoints with ID parameters 3. Replace A's ID with B's ID and observe if B's data is returned 4. Automate enumeration of sequential IDs 5. Test vertical privilege escalation: access admin APIs with a regular user token. Burp Suite Autorize plugin automates IDOR detection.
mi_en: 1. Backend must verify current user's authorization for every requested resource (based on session user_id, not request params) 2. Use UUID instead of sequential IDs 3. Implement RBAC or ABAC access control 4. Rate-limit sensitive operations to prevent bulk enumeration 5. Use Burp Autorize plugin for automated IDOR testing in development.

ov_en: Race condition vulnerabilities exploit the time window between Check and Use (TOCTOU) on the server side. When multiple concurrent requests arrive simultaneously, the server may pass a check multiple times before consuming a resource, causing resources to be consumed repeatedly. Common in e-commerce, finance, and social platforms involving limited resource operations.
vu_en: Root cause: no atomic guarantee on critical business operations. Typical TOCTOU flow: (1) Server checks if user already claimed coupon → passes; (2) Before recording 'claimed', another request also passes the check; (3) Both requests successfully claim the coupon. Missing row/optimistic locks at DB layer and missing distributed locks at application layer are primary causes.
ex_en: 1. Use Burp Turbo Intruder gate mechanism or Python asyncio for high-concurrency requests 2. HTTP/2 multiplexing achieves extreme concurrency on a single connection 3. Observe if successful responses exceed the expected limit 4. Focus on coupon claiming, balance withdrawal, points redemption, flash sales, CAPTCHA verification. Single Packet Attack (2023) is a highly efficient race exploitation technique.
mi_en: 1. Use SELECT FOR UPDATE row lock or optimistic lock (version number) at DB layer 2. Use Redis distributed lock (SETNX) for atomicity at application layer 3. Generate idempotency key per operation—duplicate requests return same result 4. Use message queue to serialize critical operations 5. Complete check and execute within a transaction to eliminate TOCTOU window.

ov_en: Payment logic vulnerabilities are among the most severe business logic flaws in e-commerce and financial systems. Attackers intercept and modify client-sent payment parameters (price, quantity, shipping, discount) or forge third-party payment platform callback notifications, achieving zero-cost purchases, negative-price profit, or payment bypass. Economic impact is typically direct.
vu_en: Root causes: (1) Frontend computes price but backend does not revalidate—trusting client-submitted amounts; (2) No range validation on quantities/amounts (negative, zero, extreme values); (3) Payment callback signature not verified or verification logic flawed; (4) Coupon system allows stacking; (5) Order amount vs actual payment amount consistency check missing. Many developers incorrectly believe HTTPS encryption prevents tampering.
ex_en: 1. Intercept order request with Burp Suite and modify price/quantity/discount fields 2. Test boundary values: 0, negative, extreme large, float, scientific notation 3. Check if payment callback endpoint is directly accessible and forgeable 4. Test coupon ID substitution and stacking 5. Check if order state machine can skip the payment step to 'paid'. Focus on mobile APIs which often have weaker validation.
mi_en: 1. Server must re-query price by product ID and compute total amount—never trust client-submitted amounts 2. Strict range validation on all numeric parameters (>0 and <MAX) 3. Payment callbacks must verify signature and validate amount matches order 4. Use DB transactions for atomic coupon deduction 5. Enforce strict order state machine to prevent state skipping.

ov_en: Password reset is one of the most critical authentication flows in web applications. Attackers exploit logic flaws via Host header injection to steal reset tokens, brute-force short verification codes, manipulate HTTP responses to deceive the frontend, or predict reset tokens from weak randomness—all enabling arbitrary account takeover.
vu_en: Common flaws: (1) Reset email/SMS constructs link URL from Host header instead of hardcoded domain; (2) Verification code has no expiry or attempt limit (4-digit code has only 10,000 possibilities); (3) Frontend uses a code field in the response to determine verification result instead of server-side session state; (4) Reset token generated with predictable algorithm (MD5(timestamp+email)); (5) Token has no expiry or single-use limit.
ex_en: (1) Host injection: modify Host/X-Forwarded-Host to attacker domain, receive token-containing request on attacker server; (2) Code brute force: Burp Intruder with Pitchfork mode enumerating 0000-9999; (3) Response manipulation: intercept failure response and modify to success to deceive frontend; (4) Token analysis: collect multiple tokens, analyze patterns, construct token for target user. Multiple techniques can be combined.
mi_en: (1) Hardcode application domain in reset links, never derive from HTTP headers; (2) 6+ digit codes, 5-minute expiry, 5-failure lockout; (3) Auth state changes (e.g., verification passed) recorded only in server-side session, not client-dependent; (4) Use crypto.randomBytes(32) CSPRNG for token generation; (5) Tokens invalidated immediately after single use, 15-minute expiry.

ov_en: CAPTCHA is a core mechanism against automated attacks, but real deployments have numerous logic flaws. Common bypass methods: CAPTCHA answer leaked in response, token reuse after verification, parameter deletion, universal debug codes, and OCR auto-recognition. Bypassing CAPTCHA enables brute force, bulk registration, and automated abuse.
vu_en: Common flaws: (1) CAPTCHA answer leaked via API response, Cookie, or JS variables; (2) CAPTCHA not invalidated server-side after verification—same code reusable; (3) Backend treats CAPTCHA validation as optional—omitting the parameter skips it; (4) Debug universal codes (e.g., 000000) not removed before production; (5) Simple image CAPTCHA easily read by OCR; (6) SMS CAPTCHA has long expiry (>5 min) or no attempt limit.
ex_en: 1. Check full response after sending CAPTCHA request (including Headers and Cookies) 2. Obtain one correct CAPTCHA and attempt to reuse it 3. Delete captcha field from request or set it empty 4. Try common universal codes: 0000/1234/8888 5. For image CAPTCHA, use ddddocr or TrueCaptcha API 6. Integrate above methods into Burp Intruder or Python script for automated bypass+brute force.
mi_en: (1) Generate and verify CAPTCHA server-side only, never return answer via any channel; (2) Invalidate CAPTCHA immediately after single use; (3) Require CAPTCHA parameter to be present and non-empty; (4) Remove all debug backdoors and universal codes; (5) Use high-complexity CAPTCHA (reCAPTCHA v3/hCaptcha) or behavioral verification; (6) SMS CAPTCHA: 6 digits, 3-minute expiry, 5-failure lockout for 30 minutes.
